Taiwan Imposes Tariffs on Imported Books, Shaking Local Publishing Sector

Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs this week imposed a 15% tariff on all imported books and periodicals, a move officials say is intended to bolster the domestic Media & Publishing industry amid mounting international competition. The measure, announced on Monday, has already begun to reshape the sector, with publishers, bookstores, and industry workers scrambling to adapt.

Local publishers report a surge in orders as schools, libraries, and individual readers turn to domestically produced titles. Chen Ming-hua, spokesperson for the Taiwan Publishing Association, noted, “We are seeing a significant uptick in inquiries and pre-orders for Taiwanese-authored content. This policy is giving our industry a much-needed boost.”

However, some industry players warn of challenges ahead. Smaller firms that previously relied on distributing international bestsellers are now facing squeezed margins and operational uncertainty. “We have had to suspend planned releases of several foreign titles due to the sudden cost increase,” said Lin Hui-jen, managing director of Green Leaf Books, a mid-sized publisher based in Taichung. “Our editorial and sales teams are working overtime to revise catalogs and negotiate with partners.”

Major printing sites across Taipei and Kaohsiung have reported rising demand, leading to extended shifts for production staff. According to the Taiwan Media Workers’ Union, job postings in editorial, translation, and printing roles have increased by 12% since the announcement.

Analysts caution that while the tariff may strengthen local firms in the short term, it could limit access to diverse content. “It’s a balancing act,” said analyst David Sung. “The long-term effects on creativity and readership remain to be seen.” The measure is scheduled for review in six months.
